entry: Indian actor, philanthropist and former politician in Telugu cinema. Known as Mega Star, he made his acting debut in 1978 and became a leading star after the 1983 film *Khaidi*. In 1998 he founded the Chiranjeevi Charitable Trust, which operates the largest blood and eye banks in the Telugu states. He founded the Praja Rajyam Party in 2008, and it merged with the [[Indian National Congress]] in 2011. In 2024 Guinness World Records recognized him as the most prolific actor-dancer in the Indian film industry.

Form of [[Alternative medicine|alternative medicine]] concerned with manual spinal therapy for mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system. Most patients seek it for low back pain. D. D. Palmer founded chiropractic in the 1890s, and its foundations, including vertebral subluxation, are at odds with evidence-based medicine. A 2011 review of 45 systematic reviews found that spinal manipulation had not been convincingly shown to be effective for any condition. Cervical manipulation has been linked to [[Stroke|stroke]], and its safety is not well established.

Hand tool with a wedge-shaped cutting edge at the end of its blade, used for carving or cutting hard materials such as wood, stone or metal. Using a chisel involves forcing the blade into the material, driven by hand pressure or by a [[Hammer|mallet or hammer]]; in industrial use, a hydraulic ram or falling weight may drive it. A gouge is a type of chisel that carves small pieces, particularly in [[Woodworking|woodworking]], woodturning and [[Sculpture|sculpture]]. Woodworking chisels include firmer, mortise, paring and dovetail types. Cold chisels, made of tempered steel, remove waste metal when a smooth finish is not required, and they are used in [[Metalworking|metalworking]].

Long-chain [[Polymer|polymer]] of N-acetylglucosamine, an amide derivative of glucose. Chitin is the second most abundant polysaccharide in nature, behind only [[Cellulose|cellulose]]; an estimated 1 billion tons are produced each year. It is a primary component of [[Cell wall|cell walls]] in fungi and of the exoskeletons of [[Arthropod|arthropods]] such as [[Crustacean|crustaceans]] and [[Insect|insects]]. Commercially it is extracted from the shells of crabs, shrimps and lobsters, which are by-products of the seafood industry. In pure form chitin is translucent, pliable and tough; combined with [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]] in crustacean and mollusc shells, it forms a much harder composite. Chitosan, produced by deacetylating chitin with [[Sodium hydroxide|sodium hydroxide]], has biomedical uses including wound healing and drug delivery.

Port city and capital of Chittagong Division, second-largest city in [[Bangladesh]] (pop., 2022: more than 5.6 million). Home to the Port of Chittagong, the busiest port in Bangladesh, it lies on the Karnaphuli River between the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the [[Bay of Bengal]]. Its port ships goods such as tea, jute and petroleum products. Merchants from the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] established a trading post there in the 9th century, and the Nawab of Bengal ceded the port to the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] in 1793. During [[World War II]] it was a base for Allied forces in the Burma Campaign. During the [[Bangladesh Liberation War]] in 1971 it was the site of the Bangladeshi declaration of independence. Chittagong accounts for 12% of Bangladesh's GDP and 80% of its international trade.

Informal and varying code of conduct associated with medieval European [[Knight|knighthood]]. It developed in France between 1170 and 1220, combining military bravery, individual training and service to others with knightly piety and courtly manners. Its roots lie in the idealization of the [[Cavalry|cavalryman]] in the [[Carolingian Empire]], especially in [[Francia]]. It was popularized in medieval literature, notably the legends of [[King Arthur]] and the paladins of [[Charlemagne]]. The code was largely a product of the Late Middle Ages, evolving after the [[Crusades]] from an idealization of knights fighting in the Holy Land and from ideals of courtly love. The word derives from the Old French *chevalerie*, meaning horse soldiery.

Common [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infection]] caused by the bacterium *Chlamydia trachomatis*. Most infected people have no symptoms. When they occur, symptoms in women may include vaginal discharge or burning with urination, and in men discharge from the penis or pain and swelling of the testicles. Untreated infection in women can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which may lead to [[Infertility|infertility]] or [[Ectopic pregnancy|ectopic pregnancy]]. Repeated eye infections can result in trachoma, a common cause of blindness in the developing world. Chlamydia is cured with [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], typically [[Azithromycin|azithromycin]] or [[Doxycycline|doxycycline]], and is prevented by consistent [[Condom|condom]] use. It affects about 4.2% of women and 2.7% of men worldwide.

Anion of [[Chlorine|chlorine]] (Cl⁻) and the main anion present in seawater. Chloride salts such as [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]] are often soluble in water. Chloride is an essential electrolyte in all body fluids, helping maintain acid–base balance, transmit nerve impulses and regulate fluid flow in and out of cells. Seawater contains about 19,400 mg/L of chloride, while chloride minerals such as halite are abundant mainly in dry climates or deep underground. Chloride ions can be detected with silver nitrate, which forms a white silver chloride precipitate. Chloride can be oxidized, for example to chlorine gas in the chlor-alkali process, but it cannot be reduced.

Chemical element with atomic number 17 and symbol Cl, a yellow-green gas at room temperature. The second-lightest [[Halogen|halogen]], it lies between [[Fluorine|fluorine]] and bromine in the periodic table. Chlorine is extremely reactive and a strong oxidizing agent, with the highest electron affinity of any element. Free chlorine gas was recognized as a separate substance around 1630, and [[Humphry Davy|Humphry Davy]] confirmed it as an element in 1810. It is produced from brine by [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]], mainly in the chloralkali process. It is used to make a wide range of consumer products, about two-thirds of them organic chemicals such as [[Polyvinyl chloride|polyvinyl chloride]], and as a disinfectant in swimming pools. Chlorine was first used as a [[Chemical weapon|chemical weapon]] in [[World War I|World War I]]. In the form of [[Chloride|chloride ions]], it is necessary to all known species of life.

Colorless, sweet-smelling organochlorine compound, CHCl₃, also called trichloromethane. It is a volatile, dense liquid produced on a large scale as a precursor to refrigerants and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and it is a common solvent. Chloroform was used as an inhalational anesthetic from the 19th century into the first half of the 20th century. It is miscible with many solvents but only very slightly soluble in water, about 8 g/L at 20°C.

Any of several related photochemical catalysts and green [[Pigment|pigments]] found in [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]] and in the [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] of [[Algae|algae]] and plants. Chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly in the blue and red parts of the [[Electromagnetic spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]], so tissues containing it appear green. Plants have chlorophyll a and b in the photosystems that drive [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], the process that produces practically all of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. The name comes from Greek words meaning pale green and leaf. Joseph Bienaimé Caventou and Pierre Joseph Pelletier first isolated and named it in 1817, and the presence of [[Magnesium|magnesium]] in it was discovered in 1906. By 1960, [[Robert Burns Woodward|Robert Burns Woodward]] had published a total synthesis of the molecule.

Major division of [[Algae|green algae]], sister to the [[Charophyta]] within the Viridiplantae. Chlorophytes are eukaryotes that usually have a single green [[Chloroplast|chloroplast]] per cell. Their chloroplasts contain [[Chlorophyll|chlorophylls]] a and b and carotenoids such as lutein, and they store [[Starch|starch]] inside the chloroplast. Most are unicellular, but the classes Chlorophyceae and Ulvophyceae show a trend toward complex colonies and multicellularity. Many form [[Flagellate|flagellate]] cells with two or four flagella of equal length. Chlorophytes lack a chloroplast endoplasmic reticulum, which distinguishes them from other algal divisions. Asexual reproduction is widespread, through autospores, zoospores and fragmentation.

Organelle, a type of [[Plastid|plastid]], that conducts photosynthesis mostly in plant and algal cells. Chloroplasts have a high concentration of [[Chlorophyll|chlorophyll]] pigments, which capture sunlight energy and decompose water to release oxygen. The chemical energy is used in the Calvin cycle to make sugar and other organic molecules from [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Chloroplasts also carry out fatty acid and amino acid synthesis. A cell may contain one chloroplast, as in some unicellular algae, or up to 100, as in plants such as Arabidopsis and [[Wheat|wheat]]. They are thought to have evolved from a [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacterium]] engulfed by an early eukaryotic cell, and they contain their own DNA. Because the plant cell cannot make them anew, they must be inherited by each daughter cell during division.

Phenothiazine antipsychotic medication, marketed as Thorazine and Largactil among others. Developed in 1950, it was the first antipsychotic on the market and is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. It is used mainly for [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]] and other psychotic disorders, and also for the manic phase of [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]]. Its mechanism is not entirely clear, but it is believed to relate to its ability as a [[Dopamine|dopamine]] antagonist. Serious side effects may include tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Food made from roasted and ground [[Cocoa bean|cocoa beans]], the processed seeds of the cacao tree. Cocoa beans are fermented, dried, roasted and ground into chocolate liquor, which can be processed into cocoa butter and cocoa powder. Adding [[Sugar|sugar]] produces sweetened chocolate, and adding [[Milk|milk]] produces milk chocolate; cocoa butter and milk alone make white chocolate. The cacao tree was used as a food source in what is now [[Ecuador]] at least 5,300 years ago. Mesoamerican civilizations, including the [[Olmecs]], widely consumed cacao beverages, and there is evidence the Olmecs fermented the pulp into an alcoholic beverage. Chocolate reached Europe in the 16th century and remained an elite drink until the 19th century, when technological advances made it a mass-consumed solid food. Most cocoa is grown in [[West Africa|West Africa]], particularly [[Ivory Coast|Ivory Coast]] and Ghana, which contribute about 60% of the world's supply.

Musical ensemble of singers, also called a chorale or chorus. Choral music is music written or performed for such an ensemble, and choirs may sing classical or popular repertoire. Most are led by a conductor. Choirs may sing unaccompanied or with a [[Piano|piano]], [[Pipe organ|pipe organ]] or [[Orchestra|orchestra]]. Most choirs have four sections singing in [[Harmony|four-part harmony]], but there is no limit on the number of parts; Thomas Tallis wrote a 40-part motet, *Spem in alium*. The term choir is often applied to church-affiliated groups, whereas a chorus usually performs in theatres or concert halls. Conductors shape the sound of the ensemble, set the tempo and cue the beats, and in most choirs one person may fill the roles of musical director, chorusmaster and conductor.

Tamil dynasty from southern India that ruled the Chola Empire, an expansive maritime empire. The earliest datable references to the Cholas are inscriptions from the 3rd century BCE, during the reign of [[Ashoka]] of the [[Maurya Empire]]. The heartland was the fertile Kaveri River valley. The Cholas unified peninsular India south of the Tungabhadra River and held that territory as one state from 907 to 1215 CE. Under [[Rajaraja I|Rajaraja I]] and his successors, the empire became a military, economic and cultural power in [[South Asia]] and [[Southeast Asia]]. The Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur was completed in 1010 CE. The dynasty continued to govern in varying territories until the 13th century CE.

Infection of the small intestine by some strains of the bacterium *Vibrio cholerae*. The classic symptom is large amounts of watery [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], which can cause severe dehydration within hours. Symptoms start two hours to five days after exposure, and severe cholera without treatment kills about half of those affected. It spreads mainly through unsafe water and food contaminated with [[Feces|feces]], and risk factors include poor [[Sanitation|sanitation]] and poverty. Primary treatment is oral rehydration salts, with [[Zinc|zinc]] supplementation for children; severe cases may need intravenous fluids and [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]]. Oral vaccines give reasonable protection for about six months. Seven [[Pandemic|pandemics]] have occurred, the most recent beginning in 1961. The study of cholera in England by [[John Snow|John Snow]] between 1849 and 1854 contributed to [[Epidemiology|epidemiology]] through his insight that the disease spread through contaminated water.

Principal sterol of animals, biosynthesized by all animal cells and an essential component of cell membranes. It is distributed especially in the [[Brain|brain]] and [[Spinal cord|spinal cord]], and it is a precursor for [[Steroid|steroid]] hormones, bile acid and [[Vitamin D|vitamin D]]. In vertebrates, liver cells produce the greatest amounts, while astrocytes supply the brain, where cholesterol is separate from peripheral cholesterol. A 68 kg man synthesizes about 1 gram per day in a 37-step process, the first 18 steps of which form the target of statin drugs. Elevated blood levels, especially of low-density lipoprotein (LDL), may increase the risk of [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]]. Cholesterol is absent among [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]], although *Mycoplasma* requires it for growth.

Class of jawed fish with skeletons primarily composed of [[Cartilage|cartilage]] rather than bone, distinguishing them from the [[Osteichthyes|bony fishes]]. Chondrichthyes are aquatic vertebrates with paired fins, placoid scales and a conus arteriosus in the heart. They breathe through five to seven pairs of [[Gill|gills]], and because they lack bone marrow, they produce red blood cells in the [[Spleen|spleen]]. The class has two subclasses: Elasmobranchii, including [[Shark|sharks]], rays, skates and sawfish, and Holocephali, the chimaeras. Living members range from the 10 cm finless sleeper ray to the [[Whale shark|whale shark]], over 10 m long. Elasmobranchs alone account for over 1,200 species.

Municipality in southwestern China, the only inland one of China's four direct-administered municipalities (urban pop., 2024: 23.01 million). It was separated from [[Sichuan]] province on March 14, 1997, and covers an area roughly the size of [[Austria]]. Because of its classification, it is the largest city proper in the world by population, though not the most populous urban area. It was the wartime capital of the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] during the [[Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] (1937–45). Chongqing is a base for the [[Belt and Road Initiative]] and headquarters of Changan Automobile, one of China's Big Four car manufacturers. Its [[Monorail|monorail]] system is the world's longest and busiest, with 70 stations.

Shaped pair of equal-length sticks used as kitchen and eating utensils in most countries of [[East Asia]]. They originated in [[China|China]] and have been used for over three millennia in the Sinosphere, including Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Traditionally they were made of [[Bamboo|bamboo]], wood, metal, [[Ivory|ivory]] or ceramic; modern versions include [[Plastic|plastic]], stainless steel and titanium. The earliest chopsticks found are six [[Bronze|bronze]] examples, about 26 centimeters long, excavated at Anyang in Henan and dated roughly to 1200 BC, during the [[Shang dynasty|Shang dynasty]]. The earliest known textual reference is in the *Han Feizi*, written by [[Han Fei|Han Fei]] in the 3rd century BCE.

Simultaneous sounding of two or more musical notes. The most common chord has three notes and is called a triad. An arpeggio sounds the notes of a chord separately, and a series of chords is called a chord progression. The word derives from accord, which became cord in [[Middle English|Middle English]] and was respelled chord in the 17th century. Until the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]], harmony meant any combination of two notes; in the [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], three simultaneous notes came to define it. Seventh chords appeared in the 16th century, and in the Baroque era figured bass indicated the harmony above each bass note. Chords with added tones or clusters are common in [[Contemporary classical music|contemporary classical music]] and [[Jazz|jazz]], which has an especially eclectic chord vocabulary. Chords are notated with [[Roman numerals|Roman numerals]], figured bass, the Nashville Number System or alphabetical symbols.

Bilaterian animal of the phylum Chordata. All chordates possess, at some stage of life, a notochord, a hollow dorsal nerve cord, an endostyle or thyroid, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail. The phylum has three subphyla: [[Vertebrate|Vertebrata]], whose members have a skull and a spinal column; Tunicata, or sea squirts, which retain these features only as larvae; and Cephalochordata, the lancelets. Chordata is the third-largest animal phylum, behind [[Arthropod|Arthropoda]] and [[Mollusca|Mollusca]]. Of more than 81,000 living species, about half are ray-finned fishes and most of the rest are [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]]. Chordate fossils have been found from the [[Cambrian explosion|Cambrian explosion]], over 539 million years ago.

Art of designing sequences of movement for physical bodies, most commonly in [[Dance|dance]]. The word means dance-writing, from Greek roots, and it first appeared in American English dictionaries in the 1950s. The term choreographer was first used as a credit for [[George Balanchine|George Balanchine]] on the Broadway show *On Your Toes* in 1936. Earlier, choreography meant the written record of dances, later called dance notation. In the 19th century, [[Marius Petipa|Marius Petipa]] was among the romantic ballet choreographers, and [[Isadora Duncan|Isadora Duncan]] and [[Martha Graham|Martha Graham]] helped shape [[Modern dance|modern dance]]. Movement language is drawn from [[Ballet|ballet]], contemporary dance, jazz, hip hop, folk dance and [[K-pop|K-pop]]. Dances may be designed through improvisation guided by a score of directives, or through a specified sequence of movements.
